speaker: Doctor
text: I see you're experiencing double vision, difficulty climbing stairs, and weakness in your upper limbs. To narrow this down, have you noticed any difficulty with swallowing or speaking recently?

speaker: Patient
text: The double vision usually happens when I look up or down, and the weakness in my arms and legs gets worse after activity but improves if I rest. I have not noticed balance problems or numbness.

speaker: Doctor
text: That pattern of worsening with activity and relief with rest is very suggestive of a neuromuscular issue. Given your double vision triggered by looking up or down and the limb weakness, have you experienced any episodes of muscle weakness upon waking up in the morning? REQUEST TEST: Creatine_kinase; REQUEST TEST: Acetylcholine_receptor_antibodies

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Acetylcholine_Receptor_Antibodies: Present (elevated), Creatine_kinase: Normal Readings

speaker: Patient
text: I have not had recent infections or fevers, and there is no family history of neurological disease. The weakness feels symmetrical in both arms and legs. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Tuberculosis and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text: That diagnosis of Tuberculosis does not align with your symptoms of double vision and fluctuating weakness, as TB typically causes fever and weight loss rather than neuromuscular fatigue. The specific eye movement issue suggests a problem with cranial nerves III, IV, or VI, possibly due to myasthenia gravis or a brainstem lesion. Can you tell me if you experience any drooping of your eyelids (ptosis) or difficulty chewing and swallowing? REQUEST TEST: Acetylcholine_receptor_antibodies; REQUEST IMAGES: CT_Brain

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Acetylcholine_Receptor_Antibodies: Present (elevated), CT_Brain: Normal Readings

speaker: Doctor
text: DIAGNOSIS READY: Myasthenia Gravis. The elevated acetylcholine receptor antibodies combined with your fluctuating weakness, diplopia on vertical gaze, and normal CT brain confirm this neuromuscular junction disorder. The previous suspicion of tuberculosis was incorrect based on these clinical findings.
